statement: Prop 5 (manuscript eq. (13)), all n: if F_E is unsatisfiable, A_E z = 1 is solvable over F_3, and deleting any single clause makes F_E satisfiable, then the rows of A_E (restricted to the n' occurring variables) are linearly independent over F_3, so rank = |E| and |E| <= n'-1.
derivation: (1) Any F_3 dependence sum lambda_i r_i = 0 with lambda_j != 0 satisfies sum_{i != j} lambda_i = -lambda_j, using a solution z of A_E z = 1; hence every w satisfying the other rows also satisfies r_j.w = 1. (2) Minimality gives a Boolean x satisfying F_E minus clause j; then r_j.x = 1 mod 3, and since r_j.x is a sum of three 0/1 values in {0..3}, it equals 1, so x satisfies F_E, a contradiction. (3) The all-ones vector lies in ker A_E because each row sums to 3 = 0 mod 3, so dim ker >= 1 and |E| <= n'-1.

LEMMA Thm1-two-valued (manuscript eq. (3), all n>=3, E subset of T_n): F_E is satisfiable iff some z in A_E = {z in F_3^n : A_E z = 1} takes at most two values. Proof. (a) If x in {0,1}^n satisfies F_E, then each clause sum is an integer in {0..3} that is 1 mod 3, hence 1; so z = x in A_E has values in {0,1}. (b) Let z in A_E take at most two values, E nonempty (E empty: z=0). A constant value a gives clause sums 3a = 0 mod 3, not 1, so the value set is {0,1}, {0,2} or {1,2}. Case {0,1}: x = z is Boolean with clause sums 1. Case {0,2}: z = 2y, y Boolean; 2(y_a+y_b+y_c) = 1 mod 3 gives y_a+y_b+y_c = 2 exactly (range {0..3}); x = 1-y is Boolean with x_a+x_b+x_c = 1. Case {1,2}: z = 1+y; clause sum = 3 + (y_a+y_b+y_c) = 1 mod 3 gives sum y = 1 exactly; x = y. In each case x satisfies F_E. QED. Closes: none (reformulation, no open obligation).

proved_step:
statement: Lemma F_q (extension of manuscript Prop 14, eq. (40d)). Let q = p^k be a prime power and r, N >= 1 integers with r(q-1) < N. For every W in F_q^{r x N} there is z in {0,1}^N, z != 0, with Wz = 0 (the 0/1 vector is read in F_q^N).
derivation: (1) For j = 1..r put f_j(X) = sum_i W_{ji} X_i^{q-1} in F_q[X_1..X_N]. Each f_j is homogeneous of degree q-1, so sum_j deg f_j = r(q-1) < N. (2) Chevalley-Warning (valid over any finite field F_q of characteristic p): if sum_j deg f_j < N, the number of common zeros x in F_q^N of f_1..f_r is divisible by p. (3) The zero vector is a common zero, so the count is a positive multiple of p, hence at least p >= 2. Pick a common zero x != 0. (4) Set z_i = x_i^{q-1}. For x_i != 0 this is 1 (Lagrange in F_q^*), for x_i = 0 it is 0, so z in {0,1}^N, and z != 0 because x != 0. (5) (Wz)_j = sum_i W_{ji} x_i^{q-1} = f_j(x) = 0 for all j, so Wz = 0. QED. Remark: the prime case q = p is Prop 14; only the degree bound and the characteristic are used. Scope: linear W over F_q with r(q-1) < N; nothing on nonlinear, input-dependent or oracle-assisted updates, and nothing on manuscript eq. (8) or (40a).
closes_obligation: none (general lemma; no open obligation recorded for it)

proved_step: LEMMA (p=3, linear state, repair of manuscript Prop 14 / eq. 40d). Let W in F_3^{r x N} with N >= 2r+1. Then there is z in {0,1}^N, z != 0, with Wz = 0 and |supp z| <= 2r+1. Proof: let k = 2r+1 and W' the first k columns of W. Put P_j(X) = sum_{i<=k} W'_{ji} X_i^2 (j=1..r). Total degree 2r < k, so by Chevalley-Warning the number of common zeros in F_3^k is divisible by 3. The zero vector is one, so a nonzero common zero x exists. Set z_i = x_i^2 in {0,1} for i<=k and z_i = 0 otherwise. Then z != 0, Wz = 0, |supp z| <= k. QED. Corollary (promise restored, C=2): a t-sparse table on m variables has circuit size <= 2tm. If N = 2^m >= 2r+1 and C(2r+1)m <= s, the kernel vector z has circuit size <= s and shares its final state with the zero table, so an exact decoder with promise size s gives r >= min{2^{m-1}, ceil((s/(2m) - 1)/2)}. Scope: p=3, linear updates over F_3, exact decoders. Does not cover nonlinear or oracle-assisted updates, update time, eq. (8) or (40a). The exponential bound 2^{m-1} is NOT recovered; that needs a kernel vector of circuit size <= s with support near 2^m.

LEMMA (REPAIR of S0001 / Prop 5, manuscript eq. (13); kind LEMMA; closes: none). Let n >= 3, E a subset of T_n, and r_i in F_3^n the 0/1 incidence row of clause i in E (three ones). Assume (H1) F_E is unsatisfiable; (H2) for every j in E, F_{E minus {j}} is satisfiable; (H3) A_E z = 1 has a solution z_0 in F_3^n. Let n' be the number of variables occurring in E. Then the rows r_i (i in E) are linearly independent over F_3, so |E| = rank A_E <= n' - 1. PROOF. (a) Suppose sum_{i in E} lambda_i r_i = 0 with some lambda_j != 0. (b) Dot with z_0 (H3): r_i . z_0 = 1 for all i, so sum_i lambda_i = 0, i.e. sum_{i != j} lambda_i = -lambda_j. (c) By (H2) take x in {0,1}^n satisfying F_{E minus {j}}. For i != j the integer r_i . x lies in {0,1,2,3} and is 1 mod 3, hence equals 1. Dot the dependence with x: 0 = sum_{i != j} lambda_i + lambda_j (r_j . x) = lambda_j (r_j . x - 1), so r_j . x = 1 in F_3. The integer r_j . x in {0,1,2,3} is 1 mod 3, hence exactly 1, so x satisfies clause j. Thus x satisfies F_E, contradicting (H1). So the rows are independent and rank A_E = |E|. (d) Columns outside the n' occurring variables are zero, so rank is computed on those n' columns. Each row sums to 3 = 0 mod 3, so the all-ones vector on those columns is a nonzero kernel vector; rank <= n' - 1. Hence |E| <= n' - 1. QED. SCOPE: positive exact-one clauses over F_3 under (H1)-(H3). E empty violates (H1), so vacuous there. (H3) is used only in step (b) and is not derived here. NOT CLAIMED: any bound beyond |E| <= n'-1; nothing on manuscript eq. (8) or (40a). Proof structure is sound: (a) Assume linear dependence with lambda_j != 0. (b) Dot with z_0 satisfying A_E z = 1 gives sum lambda_i = 0, so sum_{i!=j} lambda_i = -lambda_j. (c) By minimality (H2), exists Boolean x satisfying all clauses except j. For i!=j, r_i.x = 1 exactly (as integer in {0..3} and 1 mod 3). Dotting dependence with x gives 0 = sum_{i!=j} lambda_i + lambda_j (r_j.x) = lambda_j (r_j.x - 1), so r_j.x = 1 in F_3, hence exactly 1 as integer. Thus x satisfies clause j too, contradicting (H1). proved_step:
Prop 5′ (conditional rank lemma). Let E be a minimal unsatisfiable family of positive exact-one clauses, each involving three distinct variables, and let A_E be its incidence matrix over F_3 restricted to the n′ occurring variables. If A_E z = 1 has a solution z over F_3, then rank(A_E)=|E| and |E|≤n′−1.

Proof. Suppose the rows are dependent, so Σ_i λ_i r_i=0 for coefficients λ_i∈F_3 not all zero. Choose j with λ_j≠0. Taking the dot product with z gives Σ_i λ_i=0, since r_i·z=1 for every clause. Thus Σ_{i≠j}λ_i=−λ_j. For any w satisfying r_i·w=1 for all i≠j, the dependence gives λ_j(r_j·w)=−Σ_{i≠j}λ_i(r_i·w)=−Σ_{i≠j}λ_i=λ_j, hence r_j·w=1.

By minimality, there is a Boolean assignment x satisfying every clause except j. Apply the preceding implication to x. The integer sum of the three Boolean coordinates in clause j lies in {0,1,2,3}, and is congruent to 1 modulo 3. The only such value is 1. So x satisfies clause j as well, contradicting that E is unsatisfiable. The rows are therefore independent and rank(A_E)=|E|. Each row has three 1s, whose sum is 0 in F_3, so the all-ones vector lies in ker(A_E). It is nonzero because n′≥3. Rank-nullity now gives |E|=rank(A_E)≤n′−1. QED.

proved_step:
statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the Boolean solutions (all variables in {0,1}) of the exact-one system (14)-(15) are in bijection with proper 3-colorings of G. Consequently the number of Boolean solutions equals the number of proper 3-colorings.
derivation: Given a Boolean solution, each vertex equation (14) has exactly one selected color c, defining a coloring. For each edge e={u,v} and color c, equation (15) forces y_{e,c}=1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c}. This forced value is in {0,1} exactly when x_{u,c}+x_{v,c}<=1, which for one-hot vertex indicators is equivalent to u and v not both having color c. Requiring this for all c is equivalent to the endpoints having different colors, so the coloring is proper. Conversely, from any proper 3-coloring set x_{v,c}=1 exactly at its color and set y_{e,c}=1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c}; properness ensures every y is Boolean and all equations hold. Both constructions are inverse because all x are fixed by the coloring and all y are forced by (15), proving a bijection.

statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the homogeneous kernel over F_3 of the coefficient matrix of (14)-(15) has exactly 3^(2|V|) vectors. Proof: For each vertex v choose a triple (a_v,0,a_v,1,a_v,2) with coordinate sum 0 in F_3; there are 3^2 independent choices per vertex. Define every edge coordinate by b_{uv,c}=-a_{u,c}-a_{v,c}. Then each vertex homogeneous equation holds by the triple-sum condition, and each edge homogeneous equation holds by definition. Conversely, every kernel vector must have vertex triples summing to 0 and every edge coordinate forced by that same formula. Thus these choices give a bijection between (F_3^2)^V and the kernel, proving the count.
derivation: The construction and inverse are explicit and use only the coefficient equations in (14)-(15), not claimed steps S0013 or S0016.

statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the affine system (14)-(15) over F_3 has exactly 3^(2|V|) solutions.
derivation: The manuscript's explicit particular solution p is x_{v,0}=1, x_{v,1}=x_{v,2}=0 for every vertex and y_{e,0}=-1, y_{e,1}=y_{e,2}=1 for every edge. Translation by p is a bijection between the homogeneous kernel and the affine solution set, with inverse subtraction of p. In the homogeneous kernel, each vertex triple has coordinate sum zero, so its first two coordinates are arbitrary elements of F_3 and its third is forced; there are 3^2 independent choices per vertex. Every edge coordinate is forced by b_{e,c}=-a_{u,c}-a_{v,c}. Conversely these choices satisfy every homogeneous equation. Therefore the kernel and affine solution set each have 3^(2|V|) elements.

statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E), the fraction of solutions to the affine system (14)-(15) over F_3 whose coordinates all lie in {0,1} is chi_G(3)/3^(2|V|), where chi_G(3) denotes the number of proper 3-colorings of G.
derivation: For each vertex, the affine equation requires its three coordinates to sum to 1 in F_3. There are nine such triples, of which exactly three are Boolean: the one-hot triples. Choosing a Boolean triple at each vertex selects a color. For each edge and color, equation (15) uniquely forces y=1-x_u-x_v in F_3. This value is Boolean for all colors exactly when the endpoints have different selected colors: if both select the same color then the corresponding slack is -1=2, not Boolean; otherwise all slacks are 0 or 1. Hence Boolean affine solutions are in bijection with proper 3-colorings. The affine system has 3^(2|V|) solutions by the recorded affine-count argument (S0018); equivalently, each vertex triple has nine choices and every edge coordinate is forced. Dividing the Boolean-solution count chi_G(3) by the total gives the claimed fraction.

statement: For every finite simple graph G=(V,E) and every finite field F_q of characteristic greater than 3, the affine system (14)-(15) over F_q has q^(2|V|) solutions, exactly chi_G(3) of which have every coordinate in {0,1}.
derivation: For each vertex, choose x_{v,0},x_{v,1} freely and let equation (14) force x_{v,2}; this gives q^2 choices per vertex. Every edge coordinate is uniquely forced by (15), so there are q^(2|V|) total solutions. Since char(F_q)>3, a triple of Boolean coordinates sums to 1 in F_q exactly when its integer sum is 1, so Boolean vertex triples are precisely the one-hot triples and select a color. The forced edge slack 1-x_{u,c}-x_{v,c} is Boolean for all colors exactly when the endpoints select different colors. Thus Boolean solutions correspond bijectively to proper 3-colorings, giving exactly chi_G(3) Boolean solutions.

Lemma (forest count for the manuscript encoding). Let G=(V,E) be a finite forest, with c connected components and n=|V|. For the Boolean exact-one system (14)-(15), the number of solutions is 3^c 2^(n-c). Proof: By the encoding bijection to proper 3-colorings, it suffices to count colorings componentwise. In each tree component choose a root: it has 3 choices. Orient every edge away from the root. Each non-root vertex has exactly one parent, and once the parent color is fixed, it has exactly 2 choices different from that color; because a tree has no other already-colored neighbor, these choices are independent. Thus a tree on t vertices has 3*2^(t-1) proper 3-colorings. Multiplying over components gives product_i 3*2^(t_i-1)=3^c 2^(n-c). Isolated vertices are included as one-vertex trees and contribute 3. This establishes the claimed exact solution count for every forest, including the empty forest (n=c=0, count 1).

proved_step:
statement: For every finite forest G=(V,E) with n vertices and c connected components, and every integer q>=1, the number of proper q-colorings of G is q^c(q-1)^(n-c), with the empty forest count interpreted as 1.
derivation: Proof: In each component choose a root and orient edges away from it. Each root has q choices. For each non-root vertex, after its parent is colored, exactly q-1 colors remain available. Since a forest has a unique root-to-vertex path and no additional edges between already assigned vertices that impose new constraints at this stage, these choices are independent in a root-first ordering. A component with t vertices therefore has q(q-1)^(t-1) colorings. Multiplying over components gives q^c(q-1)^(sum_i(t_i-1))=q^c(q-1)^(n-c). For the empty forest the unique empty coloring gives 1.

evidence: The cited counterexample E={012,013,023,123} fails the stated affine-solvability hypothesis: summing its four equations gives 0=1 in F_3. Under the hypotheses, suppose a nonzero row dependence has coefficient lambda_j != 0. Pairing the dependence with a solution of A_E z=1 gives sum_i lambda_i=0. For a Boolean assignment satisfying every clause except j, the dependence then forces r_j·x=1 in F_3. Since r_j·x is an integer in {0,1,2,3}, congruence to 1 modulo 3 forces r_j·x=1, so this assignment satisfies clause j too, contradicting unsatisfiability. Thus the rows are independent. The all-ones vector is in the kernel because each row has three ones, so rank |E|<=n'-1. This verifies the conditional statement; the counterexample does not refute it.

proved_step:
statement: Cactus coloring product lemma. Let G be a finite cactus graph (each edge belongs to at most one simple cycle), with connected components G_1,...,G_c. For any integer q>=2, the number of proper q-colorings is the product over components of q times the product over their blocks B of P_B(q)/q, where P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1) for a cycle block of length ell. The empty graph has one coloring.
evidence: Proof: In a connected cactus, the incidence graph of blocks and articulation vertices is a tree. Root it at any block and choose a coloring of the root, with P_root(q) choices. Each later block meets the exposed subgraph at one articulation vertex. Color symmetry implies exactly P_B(q)/q extensions for each fixed color at that vertex. The block tree ensures new blocks add disjoint vertices and impose no other constraints. Multiplying gives q times the product of P_B(q)/q over blocks. A bridge has q(q-1) colorings. A cycle of length ell has tr((J-I)^ell)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1), since J-I has eigenvalues q-1 once and -1 with multiplicity q-1. Components color independently; the empty graph has one coloring. The proof-state response showed no matching open obligation id, so this lemma does not claim to close a pre-recorded obligation.

statement: Polynomial cactus chromatic formula. Let G be a finite cactus graph with connected components G_1,...,G_c, and let B range over all its blocks; write ell(B) for the cycle length of a cycle block. As a polynomial identity in Z[q], its chromatic polynomial is chi_G(q)= product_{i=1}^c [ q * product_{B in blocks(G_i)} (P_B(q)/q) ], where P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell(B)+(-1)^ell(B)(q-1) for a cycle block. The empty graph has chromatic polynomial 1.
evidence: Proof: For every integer q>=2, the block-cut incidence graph of each connected cactus is a tree. Root it at a block. Starting with a coloring of the root block, expose blocks in tree order; each new block meets the already exposed graph at exactly its parent articulation vertex and has no other previously exposed vertices. For any fixed color at this vertex, the number of proper extensions to the new block is P_B(q)/q: color permutations act transitively on the q possible fixed colors, and summing the extension counts over all q colors gives P_B(q), the total number of colorings of B. The bridge and cycle formulas for P_B(q) follow respectively from q(q-1) and tr((J-I)^ell)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1). Thus the displayed identity holds for every integer q>=2. Each cycle quotient P_B(q)/q is an integer polynomial, as follows from P_B(q)/q=sum_{j=0}^{ell-1}(-1)^j(q-1)^(ell-1-j). Both sides are therefore polynomials and, since they agree at infinitely many integers, are identical. Components color independently; the empty graph has polynomial 1. This closes no pre-recorded PNP-001 obligation.

statement: Corrected polynomial cactus chromatic formula. Let G be a finite cactus graph, with connected components G_i and blocks B. For each cycle block B of length ell>=3 set C_B(q)=sum_{j=0}^{ell-2}(-1)^j(q-1)^(ell-1-j); for each bridge block set C_B(q)=q-1. Then in Z[q], chi_G(q)=product_i [q * product_{B in blocks(G_i)} C_B(q)]. The empty graph has chromatic polynomial 1.
evidence: Proof: For each integer q>=2, root the block-cut tree of a connected cactus at a block and expose blocks in tree order. Each added block meets the exposed graph only at its parent articulation vertex. Color permutations act transitively on the q choices for that vertex, so the number of extensions for any fixed color is the block's chromatic polynomial divided by q. A bridge contributes q(q-1), hence quotient q-1. A cycle of length ell contributes (q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1). Writing x=q-1, this is x(x^(ell-1)+(-1)^ell); division by q=x+1 gives sum_{j=0}^{ell-2}(-1)^j x^(ell-1-j), as is verified by multiplying the finite alternating sum by x+1. Thus the product formula holds for every integer q>=2. Each factor is in Z[q], and the two sides are polynomials agreeing at infinitely many integers, so they are identical. Components color independently; the empty graph has polynomial 1. Repair note: the expansion recorded in S0029 used upper index ell-1, adding an erroneous final constant term; the corrected upper index is ell-2.

statement: Cactus coloring product lemma. For every finite cactus graph G with connected components G_i and every integer q>=2, the number of proper q-colorings is the product over components of q times the product over blocks B of P_B(q)/q, where P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1) for a cycle block of length ell; the empty graph has one coloring.
derivation: For a cycle block of length ell, proper colorings are closed walks in the loopless complete graph on q colors, hence their count is tr((J-I)^ell). The eigenvalues of J-I are q-1 with multiplicity one and -1 with multiplicity q-1, giving P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell+(-1)^ell(q-1). A bridge has q(q-1) colorings. In a connected cactus, the block-articulation incidence graph is a tree. Root it at a block. The root has P_B(q) colorings. Each child block meets the exposed subgraph at exactly its parent articulation vertex, and its remaining vertices are new. Color-permutation symmetry implies that for each fixed color at that vertex the block has exactly P_B(q)/q extensions. The block tree ensures there are no other constraints from the exposed subgraph. Multiplying the root count and all extension factors proves the connected formula. Different components color independently; the empty graph has one coloring.

statement: Lemma (rooted cactus block extension product). Let G be a finite connected cactus graph. Root its block-articulation incidence tree at a block. For each block B, let P_B(q) be its number of proper q-colorings. The number of proper q-colorings of G equals q times the product, over blocks B, of P_B(q)/q, for every integer q>=2. In particular P_B(q)=q(q-1) for a bridge block and P_B(q)=(q-1)^ell+(q-1)(-1)^ell for a cycle block of length ell.
derivation: Proof. The root block has P_B(q) colorings. Add remaining blocks in incidence-tree order. Each new block meets the already colored subgraph at exactly one articulation vertex, and its other vertices are new. For any fixed color at that articulation, the number of proper extensions into B is P_B(q)/q: color permutations act transitively on the q colors at the articulation, so the P_B(q) colorings split equally among its q possible colors. Thus each new block multiplies the count by P_B(q)/q. The root factor is P_root(q), so the total is q times the product over all blocks of P_B(q)/q. For a bridge, P_B(q)=q(q-1). For a cycle of length ell, set A=J-I, the adjacency matrix of the q-coloring graph. Proper colorings correspond to closed walks, so P_B(q)=tr(A^ell). The eigenvalues of A are q-1 once and -1 with multiplicity q-1, giving the stated expression. The empty graph separately has one coloring.

statement: For every finite graph G with treewidth k, tw(G[K_2]) <= 2k+1.
derivation: Take a tree decomposition (T,{B_t}) of G of width k. Replace each bag B_t with B'_t=B_t×{0,1}. For each original vertex v, the bags containing either of its two copies are exactly the original bags containing v, a connected subtree. Every edge inside the pair replacing v is covered by any bag containing v. Every edge between the pairs replacing adjacent u,v is covered by a bag whose original bag contains u,v. Thus the replaced bags form a tree decomposition of G[K_2], with size at most 2(k+1), so width at most 2k+1.

statement: For every finite graph G with pathwidth p, pw(G[K_2]) <= 2p+1. Proof: Let (B_1,...,B_r) be a path decomposition of G of width p. Replace each bag B_i by B_i x {0,1}. Each vertex-copy pair occurs on exactly the index interval of its original vertex, so the interval condition holds. Every blow-up edge either joins the two copies of one vertex v, covered by any original bag containing v, or joins copies of adjacent vertices u,v, covered by an expanded original bag containing u,v. Thus the expanded sequence is a path decomposition. Each expanded bag has size at most 2(p+1), hence width at most 2p+1.

statement: For every nonempty finite graph H of treewidth k and integer d>=1, tw(H[K_d]) <= d(k+1)-1.
derivation: Take a tree decomposition (T,B) of H with |B_t|<=k+1. Set B'_t=B_t×[d]. For each (v,i), its bags are exactly those containing v, hence form a nonempty connected subtree. Edges inside a fiber over v are covered by any bag containing v. Edges between fibers over uv are covered by a bag containing u,v. Thus (T,B') is a decomposition of H[K_d], with bags of size at most d(k+1), proving the bound.
